entries.59d88a5f57581eeb9cfc1b0a8d4d3f9ec5150716: <div sID="gen12193" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="95" osisID="Ps.95" sID="Ps.95"/> <div eID="gen12193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12194" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12195" type="x-p"/> For the expounding of this psalm we may borrow a great deal of light from the apostle's discourse, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.1-Heb.4.16">Heb. iii. and iv.</reference>, where it appears both to have been penned by David and to have been calculated for the days of the Messiah; for it is there said expressly (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.7">Heb. iv. 7</reference>) that the day here spoken of (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">ver. 7</reference>) is to be understood of the gospel day, in which God speaks to us by his Son in a voice which we are concerned to hear, and proposes to us a rest besides that of Canaan. In singing psalms it is intended, I. That we should "make melody unto the Lord;" this we are here excited to do, and assisted in doing, being called upon to praise God (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.1-Ps.95.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) as a great God (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.3-Ps.95.5">ver. 3-5</reference>) and as our gracious benefactor, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.6-Ps.95.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. II. That we should teach and admonish ourselves and one another; and we are here taught and warned to hear God's voice (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">ver. 7</reference>), and not to harden our hearts, as the Israelites in the wilderness did (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.8-Ps.95.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), lest we fall under God's wrath and fall short of his rest, as they did, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.10-Ps.95.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. This psalm must be sung with a holy reverence of God's majesty and a dread of his justice, with a desire to please him and a fear to offend him.
entries.692da1711dcfe9ed933c45dd6d0e1ed09a3ca1ce: <div eID="gen12195" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12194" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Invitation to Praise God; Motives to Praise.</title> <div sID="gen12196" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O come, let us sing unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. <hi type="super">2</hi> Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> a great God, and a great King above all gods. <hi type="super">4</hi> In his hand <hi type="italic">are</hi> the deep places of the earth: the strength of the hills <hi type="italic">is</hi> his also. <hi type="super">5</hi> The sea <hi type="italic">is</hi> his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry <hi type="italic">land.</hi> <hi type="super">6</hi> O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our maker. <hi type="super">7</hi> For he <hi type="italic">is</hi> our God; and we <hi type="italic">are</hi> the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. <div eID="gen12196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12197" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here, as often elsewhere, stirs up himself and others to praise God; for it is a duty which ought to be performed with the most lively affections, and which we have great need to be excited to, being very often backward to it and cold in it. Observe, <div eID="gen12197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12198" type="x-p"/> I. How God is to be praised. 1. With holy joy and delight in him. The praising song must be <hi type="italic">a joyful noise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.95.1">v. 1</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Ps.95.2">v. 2</reference>. Spiritual joy is the heart and soul of thankful praise. It is the will of God (such is the condescension of his grace) that when we give glory to him as a being infinitely perfect and blessed we should, at the same time, <hi type="italic">rejoice in him</hi> as our Father and King, and a God in covenant with us. 2. With humble reverence, and a holy awe of him (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let us worship, and bow down, and kneel before him,</hi> as becomes those who know what an infinite distance there is between us and God, how much we are in danger of his wrath and in need of his mercy." Though <hi type="italic">bodily exercise,</hi> alone, <hi type="italic">profits little,</hi> yet certainly it is our duty to glorify God with our bodies by the outward expressions of reverence, seriousness, and humility, in the duties of religious worship. 3. We must praise God with our voice; we must speak forth, sing forth, his praises out of the abundance of a heart filled with love, and joy, and thankfulness—<hi type="italic">Sing to the Lord; make a noise, a joyful noise to him, with psalms</hi>—as those who are ourselves much affected with his greatness and goodness, are forward to own ourselves so, are desirous to be more and more affected therewith, and would willingly be instrumental to kindle and inflame the same pious and devout affection in others also. 4. We must praise God in concert, in the solemn assemblies: "<hi type="italic">Come, let us sing;</hi> let us join in singing to the Lord; not others without me, nor I alone, but others with me. <hi type="italic">Let us come</hi> together <hi type="italic">before his presence,</hi> in the courts of his house, where his people are wont to attend him and to expect his manifestations of himself." Whenever we come into God's presence we must come with thanksgiving that we are admitted to such a favour; and, whenever we have thanks to give, we must <hi type="italic">come before God's presence,</hi> set ourselves before him, and present ourselves to him in the ordinances which he has appointed. <div eID="gen12198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12199" type="x-p"/> II. Why God is to be praised and what must be the matter of our praise. We do not want matter; it were well if we did not want a heart. We must praise God, <div eID="gen12199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12200" type="x-p"/> 1. Because he is <hi type="italic">a great God,</hi> and sovereign Lord of all, <reference osisRef="Ps.95.3">v. 3</reference>. He is great, and therefore <hi type="italic">greatly to be praised.</hi> He is infinite and immense, and has all perfection in himself. (1.) He has great power: <hi type="italic">He is a great King above all gods,</hi> above all deputed deities, all magistrates, to whom he said, <hi type="italic">You are gods</hi> (he manages them all, and serves his own purposes by them, and to him they are all accountable), above all counterfeit deities, all pretenders, all usurpers; he can do that which none of them can do; he can, and will, famish and vanquish them all. (2.) He has great possessions. This lower world is here particularly specified. We reckon those great men who have large territories, which they call their own against all the world, which yet are a very inconsiderable part of the universe: how great then is that God whose <hi type="italic">the whole earth is, and the fulness thereof,</hi> not only under whose feet it is, as he has an incontestable dominion over all the creatures and a propriety in them, but in whose hand it is, as he has the actual directing and disposing of all (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.4">v. 4</reference>); even <hi type="italic">the deep places of the earth,</hi> which are out of our sight, subterraneous springs and mines, <hi type="italic">are in his hand;</hi> and <hi type="italic">the height of the hills</hi> which are out of our reach, whatever grows or feeds upon them, <hi type="italic">is his also.</hi> This may be taken figuratively: the meanest of the children of men, who are as the low places of the earth, are not beneath his cognizance; and the greatest, who are as the strength of the hills, are not above his control. Whatever strength is in any creature it is derived from God and employed for him (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sea is his,</hi> and all that is in it (the waves fulfil his word); it is his, for <hi type="italic">he made it,</hi> gathered its waters and fixed its shores; <hi type="italic">the dry land,</hi> though given to the children of men, is his too, for he still reserved the property to himself; it is his, for <hi type="italic">his hands formed</hi> it, when his word made <hi type="italic">the dry land</hi> appear. His being the Creator of all makes him, without dispute, the owner of all. This being a gospel psalm, we may very well suppose that it is the Lord Jesus whom we are here taught to praise. He <hi type="italic">is a great God;</hi> the mighty God is one of his titles, and <hi type="italic">God over all, blessed for evermore.</hi> As Mediator, he is <hi type="italic">a great King above all gods;</hi> by him kings reign; and angels, principalities, and powers, are subject to him; <hi type="italic">by him,</hi> as the eternal Word, <hi type="italic">all things were made</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.3">John i. 3</reference>), and it was fit he should be the restorer and reconciler of all who was the Creator of all, <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col. i. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">20</reference>. To him all power is given both in heaven and in earth, and into his hand all things are delivered. It is he that sets one foot on the sea and the other on the earth, as sovereign Lord of both (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.2">Rev. x. 2</reference>), and therefore to him we must sing our songs of praise, and before him we must <hi type="italic">worship and bow down.</hi> <div eID="gen12200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12201" type="x-p"/> 2. Because he is our God, not only has a dominion over us, as he has over all the creatures, but stands in special relation to us (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">He is our God,</hi> and therefore it is expected we should praise him; who will, if we do not? What else did he make us for but that we should <hi type="italic">be to him for a name and a praise?</hi> (1.) He is our Creator, and the author of our being; we must <hi type="italic">kneel before the Lord our Maker,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.95.6">v. 6</reference>. Idolaters kneel before gods which they themselves made; we kneel before a God who made us and all the world and who is therefore our rightful proprietor; for his we are, and not our own. (2.) He is our Saviour, and the author of our blessedness. He is here called <hi type="italic">the rock of our salvation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.1">v. 1</reference>), not only the founder, but the very foundation, of that work of wonder, on whom it is built. <hi type="italic">That rock is Christ;</hi> to him therefore we must sing our songs of praises, <hi type="italic">to him that sits upon the throne and to the Lamb.</hi> (3.) We are therefore his, under all possible obligations: <hi type="italic">We are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand.</hi> All the children of men are so; they are fed and led by his Providence, which cares for them, and conducts them, as the shepherd the sheep. We must praise him, not only because he made us, but because he preserves and maintains us, and our breath and ways are in his hand. All the church's children are in a special manner so; Israel <hi type="italic">are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand;</hi> and therefore he demands their homage in a special manner. The gospel church is his flock. Christ is the great and good Shepherd of it. We, as Christians, are led by his hand into the green pastures, by him we are protected and well provided for, to his honour and service we are entirely devoted as a peculiar people, and therefore to him must be <hi type="italic">glory in the churches</hi> (whether it be in the world or no) <hi type="italic">throughout all ages,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.21">Eph. iii. 21</reference>.

entries.1f4fe259a6a387b9a85ddfef4ee001ea48cc2ea1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6608"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 95</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.95.1-Ps.95.11">Psa 95:1-11</reference>. David (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.7">He 4:7</reference>) exhorts men to praise God for His greatness, and warns them, in God's words, against neglecting His service.</title> <div sID="gen10123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6608"/>1. The terms used to express the highest kind of joy.<div eID="gen10123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rock--</hi>a firm basis, giving certainty of salvation (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.7">Psa 62:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10124" type="x-p"/>
entries.eedf8f4ff5a5570e44ef439d4969072630e453f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6609"/><div sID="gen10125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6609"/><hi type="bold">2. come ... presence--</hi>literally, "approach," or, meet Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Psa 17:13</reference>). <div eID="gen10125" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0477c7d50b96d4a8f14d73bbca4094fc7f86850: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6610"/><div sID="gen10126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6610"/><hi type="bold">3. above ... gods--</hi>esteemed such by men, though really nothing (<reference osisRef="Jer.5.7">Jr 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.10-Jer.10.15">10:10-15</reference>). <div eID="gen10126" type="x-p"/>
entries.191b1fd3cb22753a6840c24c1ec42f9e4472130d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6611"/><div sID="gen10127" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6611"/>4-5. The terms used describe the world in its whole extent, subject to God. <div eID="gen10127" type="x-p"/>
entries.7478a89b7b29b9ec4455a340fc6d68d08bf2c929: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6612"/><div sID="gen10128" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6612"/><hi type="bold">6. come--</hi>or, "enter," with solemn forms, as well as hearts. <div eID="gen10128" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebaace6ae42dfce1ef655e7c959a1b108ee7aa12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6613"/><div sID="gen10129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6613"/>7. This relation illustrates our entire dependence (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.23.3">Psa 23:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">74:1</reference>). The last clause is united by Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.3.7">He 3:7</reference>) to the following (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.81.8">Psa 81:8</reference>), <div eID="gen10129" type="x-p"/>
entries.b8908d7fb4b4d611736197e690bca9bb177718b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6614"/><div sID="gen10130" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6614"/>8-11. warning against neglect; and this is sustained by citing the melancholy fate of their rebellious ancestors, whose provoking insolence is described by quoting the language of God's complaint (<reference osisRef="Num.14.11">Nu 14:11</reference>) of their conduct at Meribah and Massah, names given (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.7">Ex 17:7</reference>) to commemorate their strife and contention with Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.18">Psa 78:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.41">41</reference>). <div eID="gen10130" type="x-p"/>

entries.e4061b5575a93b2567581d576440625204570b88: <div eID="gen21763" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21764" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21765" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21765" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21764" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21766" type="x-p"/> An invitation to praise God, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.1">Psa 95:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.2">Psa 95:2</reference>. The reason on which this is founded, the majesty and dominion of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.3-Psa.95.5">Psa 95:3-5</reference>. An invitation to pray to God, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.6">Psa 95:6</reference>. And the reasons on which that is founded, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.7">Psa 95:7</reference>. Exhortation not to act as their fathers had done, who rebelled against God, and were cast out of his favor, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.8-Psa.95.11">Psa 95:8-11</reference>. <div eID="gen21766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21767" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is also without a title, both in the Hebrew and Chaldee: but is attributed to David by the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Syriac; and by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.3-Heb.4.7">Heb 4:3-7</reference>. Calmet and other eminent critics believe that it was composed during the time of the captivity, and that the apostle only followed the common opinion in quoting it as the production of David, because in general the Psalter was attributed to him. <div eID="gen21767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21768" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is a solemn invitation to the people, when assembled for public worship, to praise God from a sense of his great goodness; and to be attentive to the instructions they were about to receive from the reading and expounding of the law; and or these accounts it has been long used in the Christian Church, at the commencement of public service, to prepare the people's minds to worship God in spirit and in truth. <div eID="gen21768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21769" type="x-p"/> Houbigant, and other learned divines, consider this Psalm as composed of three parts. <div eID="gen21769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21770" type="x-p"/> 1. The part of the people, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.1">Psa 95:1</reference> to the middle of <reference osisRef="Psa.95.7">Psa 95:7</reference>. <div eID="gen21770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21771" type="x-p"/> 2. The part of the priest or prophet from the middle of <reference osisRef="Psa.95.7">Psa 95:7</reference> to the end of <reference osisRef="Psa.95.8">Psa 95:8</reference>. <div eID="gen21771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21772" type="x-p"/> 3. The part of Jehovah, <reference osisRef="Psa.95.9-Psa.95.11">Psa 95:9-11</reference>. It is written as a part of the preceding Psalm by nine of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS.; but certainly it must have been originally an ode by itself, as the subject is widely different from that in the foregoing. <div eID="gen21772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21773" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21774" type="x-p"/> O come, let us sing - Let us praise God, not only with the most joyful accents which can be uttered by the voice; but let us also praise him with hearts tuned to gratitude, from a full sense of the manifold benefits we have already received. <div eID="gen21774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21775" type="x-p"/> The rock of our salvation - The strong Fortress in which we have always found safety, and the Source whence we have always derived help for our souls. In both these senses the word rock, as applied to God, is used in the Scriptures.
entries.3e66b06cb80de5be4685cf975f871f9ad47aa9b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21776" type="x-p"/> Let us come before his presence - פניו panaiv, his faces, with thanksgiving, בתודה bethodah, with confession, or with the confession-offering. Praise him for what he has all ready done, and confess your unworthiness of any of his blessings. The confession-offering, the great atoning sacrifice, can alone render your acknowledgment of sin and thanksgiving acceptable to a holy and just God.
entries.17e28b61210a1a6d13f4742eefe0afd4ccaed251: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21777" type="x-p"/> For the Lord is a great God - Or, "A great God is Jehovah, and a great King above all gods;" or, "God is a great King over all." The Supreme Being has three names here: אל El, יהוה Jehovah, אלהים Elohim, and we should apply none of them to false gods. The first implies his strength; the second his being and essence; the third, his covenant relation to mankind. In public worship these are the views we should entertain of the Divine Being.
entries.d02c7f769f2b489f03f671b3170815ad36880877: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21778" type="x-p"/> In his hand are the deep places of the earth - The greatest deeps are fathomed by him. <div eID="gen21778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21779" type="x-p"/> The strength of the hills is his also - And to him the greatest heights are accessible,
entries.b10bd88c4e8ef4e0674f0a4dea9437188ff6c1f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21780" type="x-p"/> The sea is his - The sea and the dry land are equally his, for he has formed them both, and they are his property. He governs and disposes of them as he sees good. He is the absolute Master of universal nature. Therefore there is no other object of worship nor of confidence.
entries.75681c70eaac46fb8aef9cb0c336ccdfe15360df: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21781" type="x-p"/> O come, let us worship - Three distinct words are used here to express three different acts of adoration: <div eID="gen21781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21782" type="x-p"/> 1. Let us worship, נשתחוה nishtachaveh, let us prostrate ourselves; the highest act of adoration by which the supremacy of God is acknowledged. <div eID="gen21782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21783" type="x-p"/> 2. Let us bow down, נכרעה nichraah, let us crouch or cower down, bending the legs under, as a dog in the presence of his master, which solicitously waits to receive his commands. <div eID="gen21783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21784" type="x-p"/> 3. Let us kneel, נברכה nibrachah, let us put our knees to the ground, and thus put ourselves in the posture of those who supplicate. <div eID="gen21784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21785" type="x-p"/> And let us consider that all this should be done in the presence of Him who is Jehovah our Creator.
entries.9bd20a12863b5d53f8ed3a927d012c4aa4f103c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21786" type="x-p"/> For he is our God - Here is the reason for this service. He has condescended to enter into a covenant with us, and he has taken us for his own; therefore: - <div eID="gen21786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21787" type="x-p"/> We are the people of his pasture - Or, rather, as the Chaldee, Syriac, Vulgate, and Ethiopic read, "We are his people, and the sheep of the pasture of his hand." We are his own; he feeds and governs us, and his powerful hand protects us. <div eID="gen21787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21788" type="x-p"/> To-day if ye will hear his voice - To-day-you have no time to lose; to-morrow may be too late. God calls to-day; to-morrow he may be silent. This should commence the eighth verse, as it begins what is supposed to be the part of the priest or prophet who now exhorts the people; as if he had said: Seeing you are in so good a spirit, do not forget your own resolutions, and harden not your hearts, "as your fathers did in Meribah and Massah, in the wilderness;" the same fact and the same names as are mentioned <reference osisRef="Exo.17.7">Exo 17:7</reference>; when the people murmured at Rephidim, because they had no water; hence it was called Meribah, contention or provocation, and Massah, temptation.
entries.3041aa51d21a6289c7475abf2f829452adc78d1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21789" type="x-p"/> When your fathers tempted me - Tried me, by their insolence, unbelief, and blasphemy. They proved me - they had full proof of my power to save and to destroy. There they saw my works - they saw that nothing was too hard for God.
entries.18fcc52e303d54fdc7f0aad7da278a8c21ee7b88: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21790" type="x-p"/> Forty years long - They did nothing but murmur, disbelieve, and rebel, from the time they began their journey at the Red Sea till they passed over Jordan, a period of forty years. During all this time God was grieved by that generation; yet he seldom showed forth that judgment which they most righteously had deserved. <div eID="gen21790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21791" type="x-p"/> It is a people that do err in their heart - Or, according to the Chaldee, These are a people whose idols are in their hearts. At any rate they had not God there. <div eID="gen21791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21792" type="x-p"/> They have not known my ways - The verb ידע yada, to know, is used here, as in many other parts of Scripture, to express approbation. They knew God's ways well enough; but they did not like them; and would not walk in them. "These wretched men," says the old Psalter, "were gifnen to the lufe of this lyfe: knewe noght my ways of mekenes, and charlte: for thi in my wreth I sware to thaim; that es, I sett stabely that if that sall entre in till my rest;" that is, they shall not enter into my rest. <div eID="gen21792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21793" type="x-p"/> This ungrateful people did not approve of God's ways - they did not enter into his designs - they did not conform to his commands - they paid no attention to his miracles - and did not acknowledge the benefits which they received from his hands; therefore God determined that they should not enter into the rest which he had promised to them on condition that, if they were obedient, they should inherit the promised land. So none of those who came out of Egypt, except Joshua and Caleb, entered into Canaan; all the rest died in the wilderness, wherein, because of their disobedience, God caused them to wander forty years. <div eID="gen21793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21794" type="x-p"/> It is well known that the land of Canaan was a type of heaven, where, after all his toils, the good and faithful servant is to enter into the joy of his Lord. And as those Israelites in the wilderness were not permitted to enter into the land of Canaan because of their unbelief, their distrust of God's providence, and consequent disobedience, St. Paul hence takes occasion to exhort the Jews, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.2-Heb.4.11">Heb 4:2-11</reference>, to accept readily the terms offered to them by the Gospel. He shows that the words of the present Psalm are applicable to the state of Christianity; and intimates to them that, if they persisted in obstinate refusal of those gracious offers, they likewise would fall according to the same example of unbelief - Dodd.  <chapter eID="Ps.95"/> <div eID="gen21794" type="x-p"/>

entries.9441fc189451c020ee0a502d435d0402ef48ddbc: <reference osisRef="Ps.95.1-Ps.95.2">Psa 95:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9938" type="x-p"/> Jahve is called the Rock of our salvation (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.27">Psa 89:27</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.94.22">Psa 94:22</reference>) as being its firm and sure ground. Visiting the house of God, one comes before God’s face; קדּם פּני, <hi type="italic">praeoccupare faciem</hi>, is equivalent to <hi type="italic">visere </hi>(<hi type="italic">visitare</hi>). תּודה is not <hi type="italic">confessio peccati</hi>, but <hi type="italic">laudis</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> before תודה is the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of accompaniment, as in Mic 6:6; that before זמרות (according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">2Sa 23:1</reference> a name for psalms, whilst מזמר can only be used as a technical expression) is the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the medium.
entries.8af99e4256d213d283495a936971bafa48eacf92: <reference osisRef="Ps.95.3-Ps.95.7">Psa 95:3-7</reference> <div eID="gen9938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9939" type="x-p"/> The adorableness of God receives a threefold confirmation: He is exalted above all gods as King, above all things as Creator, and above His people as Shepherd and Leader. אלהים (gods) here, as in Psa 96:4., <reference osisRef="Ps.97.7">Psa 97:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.97.9">Psa 97:9</reference>, and frequently, are the powers of the natural world and of the world of men, which the Gentiles deify and call kings (as Moloch Molech, the deified fire), which, however, all stand under the lordship of Jahve, who is infinitely exalted above everything that is otherwise called god (<reference osisRef="Ps.96.4">Psa 96:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.97.9">Psa 97:9</reference>). The supposition that תּועפות הרים denotes the pit-works (μέταλλα) of the mountains (Böttcher), is at once improbable, because to all appearance it is intended to be the antithesis to מחקרי־ארץ, the shafts of the earth. The derivation from ועף (יעף), κάμνειν, κοπιᾶν, also does not suit תועפות in Num 23:22; Num 24:8, for “fatigues” and “indefatigableness” are notions that lie very wide apart. The כּסף תּועפות of <reference osisRef="Job.22.25">Job 22:25</reference> might more readily be explained according to this “silver of fatigues,” i.e., silver that the fatiguing labour of mining brings to light, and תועפות הרים in the passage before us, with Gussetius, Geier, and Hengstenberg: <hi type="italic">cacumina montium quia defatigantur qui eo ascendunt</hi>, prop. ascendings = summits of the mountains, after which כסף תועפות, <reference osisRef="Job.22.25">Job 22:25</reference>, might also signify “silver of the mountain-heights.” But the lxx, which renders δόξα in the passages in Numbers and τὰ ὕψη τῶν ὀρέων in the passage before us, leads one to a more correct track. The verb יעף (ועף), transposed from יפע (ופע), goes back to the root יף, וף, to stand forth, tower above, to be high, according to which תועפות = תופעות signifies <hi type="italic">eminentiae</hi>, i.e., towerings = summits, or prominences = high (the highest) perfection (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.22.25">Job 22:25</reference>). In the passage before us it is a synonym of the Arabic <hi type="italic">mı̂fan , mı̂fâtun , pars terrae eminens</hi> (from Arab. <hi type="italic">wfâ</hi> = יפע, prop. instrumentally: a means of rising above, viz., by climbing), and of the names of eminences derived from Arab. <hi type="italic">yf'</hi> (after which Hitzig renders: the teeth of the mountains). By reason of the fact that Jahve is the Owner (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>), because the Creator of all things, the call to worship, which concerns no one so nearly as it does Israel, the people, which before other peoples is Jahve’s creation, viz., the creation of His miraculously mighty grace, is repeated. In the call or invitation, השׁתּחוה signifies to stretch one’s self out full length upon the ground, the proper attitude of adoration; כּרע, to curtsey, to totter; and בּרך, Arabic <hi type="italic">baraka</hi>, starting from the radical signification <hi type="italic">flectere</hi>, to kneel down, <hi type="italic">in genua</hi> (πρόχνυ, <hi type="italic">pronum</hi> = <hi type="italic">procnum</hi>) <hi type="italic">procumbere</hi>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.13">2Ch 6:13</reference> (cf. Hölemann, <hi type="italic">Bibelstudien</hi>, i. 135f.). Beside עם מרעיתו, people of His pasture, צאן ידו is not the flock formed by His creating hand (Augustine: <hi type="italic">ipse gratiâ suâ nos oves fecit</hi>), but, after <reference osisRef="Gen.30.35">Gen 30:35</reference>, the flock under His protection, the flock led and defended by His skilful, powerful hand. Böttcher renders: flock of His charge; but יד in this sense (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.3">Jer 6:3</reference>) signifies only a place, and “flock of His place” would be poetry and prose in one figure.

entries.49952e42a59edfae0dcf730ab43b53be56f15847:
PSALM 95
The inspired penman of this psalm, whoever he was,
This psalm has no inscription, but the Septuagint, Vulgate, Æthiopic, Arabic, and Syriac versions, and the apostle Paul in Hebrews 4:7, ascribe it to David; so that there can be no doubt that it is one of the compositions of the sweet singer of Israel.
in exhorting the Jews to praise God in solemn assembly, states two grounds why God should be praised; the one, that he sustains by his power the world which he created, the other, that he had of his free grace adopted the Church into a gracious relationship with himself. As many take God’s praises into their lips in a hypocritical manner, he exhorts the people at the same time to be sincere, serious, and devoted in the service, and to show by the tenor of their life that they had not been chosen in vain. The more effectually to guard them against hypocrisy, he mentions that their fathers from the beginning had been of a stubborn spirit, and chargeable with ingratitude to God; and he takes notice of the dreadful punishment which fell upon them, and which might well deter their children from following in the footsteps of their rebelliousness.
Psalm 95:1-5
1. Come, let us rejoice before Jehovah; let us make a joyful noise to the Rock of our salvation.
Horsley reads the second clause, “Let us raise the loud peal of melody to the Rock of our salvation;” on which he has the following note: “The verb הריע signifies to make a loud sound of any sort, either with the voice or with instruments. In the Psalms it generally refers to the mingled din of voices and various instruments, in the temple-service. This wide sense of the word cannot be expressed otherwise in the English language than by a peripharasis.” Bishop Mant, acting on this notion, has ventured, conformably to it, to specify in his version some of the instruments commonly used in the temple-worship: —
“Come, let us sing Jehovah’s praise! To him the pealing chorus raise, With trump, and harp, and cymbals ring; The rock on which our hopes are placed!”
2. Let us come before his face with praise, In psalms let us shout for joy unto him. 3. For Jehovah is a great God, And a great King, above all gods. 4. For in his hand are the deep places of the earth,
“The deep places of the earth,” which are opposed to the “heights of the mountains,” plainly mean the deepest and most retired parts of the terraqueous globe, which are explored by the eye of God, and by his only. Horsely reads the verse thus, —
“The God in whose hand are the nethermost recesses of the earth, Whose also are the inaccessible summits of the mountains.”
“This, and the following verse,” says he, “are expositive of the greatness of the Godship of Jehovah, generally mentioned in the lst verse. ‘The God, in whose hand.’ Thus, I have endeavoured to preserve the full force of the Hebrew phrase אשר בידו.” Bythner’s version of the last member is, “And the strength of the mountains is his.” He derives the noun ותועפות, vethoaphoth, which he renders strength, from the verb יעף, yaaph, was wearied; and observes, that this is “a noun plural feminine, weariness, — by antiphrasis, strength: is read four times in Scripture, and is said of mountains, silver, and the unicorn, the weariness and difficulty in overcoming which, denote their great strength.” Pagninus gives a similar rendering. Montanus has cacumina, the tops, which the Septuagint seems to agree, reading τὰ ὕ ψη τῶν ὀρέων.
And the heights of the mountains are his. 5. For his is the sea, and he made it; And the dry land his hands formed.
 
1. Come, let us rejoice before Jehovah. This psalm is suited for the Sabbath, when we know that the religious assemblies were more particularly convened for the worship of God. It is not individuals among the godly whom he exhorts to celebrate the divine praises in private; he enjoins these to be offered up in the public meeting. By this he showed that the outward worship of God principally consisted in the sacrifice of praise, and not in dead ceremonies. He enjoins haste upon them; by which they might testify their alacrity in this service. For the Hebrew word קדם, kadam, in the second verse, which I have rendered, let us come before, etc., means to make haste. He calls upon them to speed into the presence of God; and such an admonition was needed, considering how naturally backward we are when called by God to the exercise of thanksgiving. This indirect charge of indolence in the exercise, the Psalmist saw it necessary to prefer against God’s ancient people; and we should be made aware that there is just as much need of a stimulus in our own case, filled as our hearts are with similar ingratitude. In calling them to come before God’s face, he uses language which was also well fitted to increase the ardor of the worshippers; nothing being more agreeable than to offer in God’s own presence such a sacrifice as he declares that he will accept. He virtually thus says, in order to prevent their supposing the service vain, that God was present to witness it. I have shown elsewhere in what sense God was present in the sanctuary.
